chief_complaint: complete right facial droop, inability to close eyelid, and asymmetric smile after parotidectomy
hpi_details: 42F status post radical parotidectomy with CN VII sacrifice presenting with severe corneal exposure and inability to smile undergoing dynamic facial reanimation using free functioning gracilis muscle transfer innervated by masseteric nerve.
ideas: She knows the nerve had to be taken out during her tumor surgery and believes the facial muscles on that side are completely dead and cannot move without donor muscle.
concerns: She is terrified that her inability to close her right eye will lead to permanent blindness and feels heartbroken that she cannot smile at her children.
expectations: She hopes the specialist can perform a surgery using muscle from her leg to restore a natural smile and help her eyelid close properly.

clinical_knowledge.topic: Post-Parotidectomy Complete Facial Nerve Paralysis evaluation and management
core_concepts: Prompt recognition and structured assessment of Post-Parotidectomy Complete Facial Nerve Paralysis is essential for guiding targeted diagnostic workup and clinical decision-making.
A thorough clinical history, baseline risk assessment, and targeted objective testing must be synthesized rather than relying on any single symptom in isolation.

Standard management emphasizes Evidence-based diagnostic and therapeutic protocol for Post-Parotidectomy Complete Facial Nerve Paralysis, adapted to individual patient risk factors and clinical severity.
Diagnostic workup and therapeutic decisions should adhere to established clinical guidelines while accounting for patient-specific comorbidities.

common_misconceptions: Assuming that an atypical or mild presentation rules out Post-Parotidectomy Complete Facial Nerve Paralysis.
Relying solely on a single normal laboratory value or imaging result to prematurely exclude pathology.
Equating temporary symptomatic relief with full resolution of the underlying condition without completing standard evaluation.
Misattributing symptoms exclusively to Soft tissue infection without completing a comprehensive diagnostic workup.
dangerous_errors: Failing to recognize red-flag features and delaying urgent escalation or emergency intervention.
Prematurely discharging or reassuring the patient before completing appropriate diagnostic assessment.
Initiating empirical treatment without considering major patient contraindications or drug interactions.
Ignoring critical warning signs such as: Flap ischemia or tissue necrosis.
management_principles: Protect the cornea first (lubrication, taping or moisture chamber, upper-eyelid weight or tarsorrhaphy), then plan dynamic reanimation by free functioning gracilis transfer innervated by the masseteric nerve, with static suspension as an adjunct
Refer to specialty team and provide comprehensive patient counseling
Assess clinical stability, monitor vital parameters, and perform targeted diagnostic investigations.
Implement targeted therapeutic interventions per evidence-based clinical practice guidelines.
boundaries_and_exceptions: Specific drug dosages, monitoring protocols, and referral criteria must be tailored to organ function, comorbidities, and local hospital pathways.
Atypical presentations in elderly, pediatric, or immunocompromised patients may require lower thresholds for inpatient monitoring and specialist consultation.

differentials: Recurrent parotid malignancy involving the facial nerve trunk
Post-operative neurapraxia of a preserved but stretched branch
Failed nerve graft or failed free functioning muscle transfer
red_flags: Eye pain, redness, visual change, or inability to protect the cornea
New limb weakness, speech disturbance, severe headache, or other central neurologic symptoms

must_ask.say: When did you first notice the facial weakness after your parotid surgery?

history.answer: The entire right side of my face has been frozen and drooping ever since my salivary gland surgery, and I cannot shut my right eye or smile.
It started immediately when I woke up from my right parotid surgery three months ago, and it has not improved at all since then.
I cannot wrinkle the right side of my forehead at all, and my right eyelid will not close even when I squeeze shut as hard as I can.
No, I have full strength in both arms and both legs, and I have not felt any numbness or tingling in my limbs.
My speech sounds slightly muffled because my lips do not seal on the right side, but I do not have slurred speech, dizziness, or double vision.
No, I have not had any severe headaches, nausea, vomiting, or episodes of confusion.
No, I do not have any ear pain, and there have been no rashes or blisters in my ear or mouth.
No, I never had any pain or tenderness behind my ear before the weakness started.
No, my hearing is completely normal on both sides, with no ringing, buzzing, or spinning sensations.
No, my sense of taste is normal, and sounds do not seem unusually loud or echoing.
My right eye gets very dry, red, and gritty because it stays open all day, and tears keep running down my cheek.
Yes, water leaks out of the right corner of my mouth when I drink, and food frequently gets stuck inside my right cheek when I chew.
No, I have not had a cold, shingles, any rashes, or any history of tick bites.
No, this has never happened to me before, and the left side of my face moves completely normally.
I had a firm salivary gland tumor removed on the right side three months ago, but I do not feel any new lumps in front of or below my ear.
I have never had any head injuries; the only operation was the radical surgery to remove my right parotid gland three months ago.
No, I do not have diabetes or high blood pressure, and I am not pregnant.
I instill artificial tear drops every hour during the day, use thick lubricating gel at bedtime, and tape my right eyelid closed every night.
The right side of my face is completely paralyzed from my brow down to my chin, while the left side has full normal movement.
It is embarrassing to eat around other people, and being unable to smile has been devastating for my self-confidence and work.

I know the nerve was sacrificed when they took out the tumor, so I feel like the muscles on that side of my face are completely dead and will never work again on their own. I'm terrified I might lose my eyesight from my eye constantly drying out, and it breaks my heart every single day that I can't smile back at my kids.
I have always been healthy and have no chronic medical conditions.
Only the radical right parotidectomy three months ago, where the doctor warned me the facial nerve had to be sacrificed.
Just preservative-free lubricating eye drops and nighttime eye ointment; I take no prescription medications or supplements.
I do not have any known allergies to medications, foods, or latex.
I have never smoked cigarettes or used tobacco products, and I only drink a glass of wine once or twice a month socially.
I work as a graphic designer and live with my husband and our two teenage children.
There is no family history of facial paralysis, salivary gland tumors, or neurologic diseases.
My menstrual cycles are regular every twenty-eight days, my last period was two weeks ago, and my husband had a vasectomy, so pregnancy is not possible.

exam.finding: Alert, well-appearing woman with noticeable right facial asymmetry, flat right nasolabial fold, and right oral commissure droop at rest.
Blood pressure 118/74 mmHg, heart rate 72 beats/min, respiratory rate 14 breaths/min, body temperature 36.7 C, oxygen saturation 99% on ambient air.
Right lagophthalmos with a 4 mm eyelid gap on attempted closure, mild right conjunctival injection without corneal ulceration, and normal pupillary light responses bilaterally.
Complete right peripheral facial paralysis with absent forehead wrinkling, absent right eye closure, and inability to smile or puff the right cheek; other cranial nerves are intact.
A well-healed preauricular to cervical surgical scar on the right, with normal external auditory canals and clear tympanic membranes bilaterally without blisters or effusion.
Depression in the right parotid bed consistent with previous resection, with no palpable mass, tenderness, or enlarged cervical lymph nodes.
Normal muscle bulk and tone with full 5 out of 5 motor strength in all four extremities bilaterally.
Normal facial sensation across all trigeminal distributions, with mild sensory blunting confined strictly to the right preauricular scar margin.
Normal finger-to-nose testing and smooth, steady gait with a negative Romberg test.
